Inaugurate copy-on-write credentials management.  This uses RCU to manage the
credentials pointer in the task_struct with respect to accesses by other tasks.
A process may only modify its own credentials
column2: and so does not need locking to

column1: access or modify its own credentials.
A mutex (cred_replace_mutex) is added to the task_struct to control the effect
of PTRACE_ATTACHED on credential calculations
execve().
With this patch
column2: the contents of an active credentials struct may not be

column1: changed directly; rather a new set of credentials must be prepared
and committed using something like the following sequence of events:
struct cred *new = prepare_creds();
int ret = blah(new);
if (ret < 0) {
abort_creds(new);
return ret;
return commit_creds(new);
There are some exceptions to this rule: the keyrings pointed to by the active
credentials may be instantiated - keyrings violate the COW rule as managing
COW keyrings is tricky
column2: given that it is possible for a task to directly alter

column1: the keys in a keyring in use by another task.
To help enforce this
column2: various pointers to sets of credentials

column1: the task_struct
column2: are declared const.  The purpose of this is compile-time

column1: discouragement of altering credentials through those pointers.  Once a set of
credentials has been made public through one of these pointers
modified
(1) Its reference count may incremented and decremented.
(2) The keyrings to which it points may be modified
The only safe way to modify anything else is to create a replacement and commit
using the functions described in Documentation/credentials.txt (which will be
added by a later patch).
This patch and the preceding patches have been tested with the LTP SELinux
testsuite.
This patch makes several logical sets of alteration:
(1) execve().
This now prepares and commits credentials in various places in the
security code rather than altering the current creds directly.
(2) Temporary credential overrides.
do_coredump() and sys_faccessat() now prepare their own credentials and
temporarily override the ones currently on the acting thread
preventing interference from other threads by holding cred_replace_mutex
on the thread being dumped.
This will be replaced in a future patch by something that hands down the
credentials directly to the functions being called
the task's objective credentials.
(3) LSM interface.
A number of functions have been changed
(*) security_capset_check()
(*) security_capset_set()
Removed in favour of security_capset().
(*) security_capset()
New.  This is passed a pointer to the new creds
creds and the proposed capability sets.  It should fill in the new
creds or return an error.  All pointers
new creds
(*) security_bprm_apply_creds()
Changed; now returns a value
column2: which will cause the process to be

column1: killed if it's an error.
(*) security_task_alloc()
Removed in favour of security_prepare_creds().
(*) security_cred_free()
New.  Free security data attached to cred->security.
(*) security_prepare_creds()
New. Duplicate any security data attached to cred->security.
(*) security_commit_creds()
New. Apply any security effects for the upcoming installation of new
security by commit_creds().
(*) security_task_post_setuid()
Removed in favour of security_task_fix_setuid().
(*) security_task_fix_setuid()
Fix up the proposed new credentials for setuid().  This is used by
cap_set_fix_setuid() to implicitly adjust capabilities in line with
setuid() changes.  Changes are made to the new credentials
than the task itself as in security_task_post_setuid().
(*) security_task_reparent_to_init()
Removed.  Instead the task being reparented to init is referred
directly to init's credentials.
NOTE!  This results in the loss of some state: SELinux's osid no
longer records the sid of the thread that forked it.
(*) security_key_alloc()
(*) security_key_permission()
Changed.  These now take cred pointers rather than task pointers to
refer to the security context.
(4) sys_capset().
This has been simplified and uses less locking.  The LSM functions it
calls have been merged.
(5) reparent_to_kthreadd().
This gives the current thread the same credentials as init by simply using
commit_thread() to point that way.
(6) __sigqueue_alloc() and switch_uid()
__sigqueue_alloc() can't stop the target task from changing its creds
beneath it
column2: so this function gets a reference to the currently applicable

column1: user_struct which it then passes into the sigqueue struct it returns if
successful.
switch_uid() is now called from commit_creds()
folded into that.  commit_creds() should take care of protecting
__sigqueue_alloc().
(7) [sg]et[ug]id() and co and [sg]et_current_groups.
The set functions now all use prepare_creds()
abort_creds() to build and check a new set of credentials before applying
it.
security_task_set[ug]id() is called inside the prepared section.  This
guarantees that nothing else will affect the creds until we've finished.
The calling of set_dumpable() has been moved into commit_creds().
Much of the functionality of set_user() has been moved into
commit_creds().
The get functions all simply access the data directly.
(8) security_task_prctl() and cap_task_prctl().
security_task_prctl() has been modified to return -ENOSYS if it doesn't
want to handle a function
column2: or otherwise return the return value directly

column1: rather than through an argument.
Additionally
column2: cap_task_prctl() now prepares a new set of credentials

column1: if it doesn't end up using it.
(9) Keyrings.
A number of changes have been made to the keyrings code:
(a) switch_uid_keyring()
all been dropped and built in to the credentials functions directly.
They may want separating out again later.
(b) key_alloc() and search_process_keyrings() now take a cred pointer
rather than a task pointer to specify the security context.
(c) copy_creds() gives a new thread within the same thread group a new
thread keyring if its parent had one
keyring.
(d) The authorisation key now points directly to the credentials to extend
the search into rather pointing to the task that carries them.
(e) Installing thread
column2: process or session keyrings causes a new set of

column1: credentials to be created
column2: even though it's not strictly necessary for

column1: process or session keyrings (they're shared).
(10) Usermode helper.
The usermode helper code now carries a cred struct pointer in its
subprocess_info struct instead of a new session keyring pointer.  This set
of credentials is derived from init_cred and installed on the new process
after it has been cloned.
call_usermodehelper_setup() allocates the new credentials and
call_usermodehelper_freeinfo() discards them if they haven't been used.  A
special cred function (prepare_usermodeinfo_creds()) is provided
specifically for call_usermodehelper_setup() to call.
call_usermodehelper_setkeys() adjusts the credentials to sport the
supplied keyring as the new session keyring.
(11) SELinux.
SELinux has a number of changes
column2: in addition to those to support the LSM

column1: interface changes mentioned above:
(a) selinux_setprocattr() no longer does its check for whether the
current ptracer can access processes with the new SID inside the lock
that covers getting the ptracer's SID.  Whilst this lock ensures that
the check is done with the ptracer pinned
until the lock is released
column2: so there's no point doing it inside the

column1: lock.
(12) is_single_threaded().
This function has been extracted from selinux_setprocattr() and put into
a file of its own in the lib/ directory as join_session_keyring() now
wants to use it too.
The code in SELinux just checked to see whether a task shared mm_structs
with other tasks (CLONE_VM)
column2: but that isn't good enough.  We really want

column1: to know if they're part of the same thread group (CLONE_THREAD).
(13) nfsd.
The NFS server daemon now has to use the COW credentials to set the
credentials it is going to use.  It really needs to pass the credentials
down to the functions it calls
column2: but it can't do that until other patches

column1: in this series have been applied.
